2023A-p3#x: Randomly assign each vertex to one of three parts and define an indicator that an edge crosses between parts.

Compute one edge's crossing probability, then derandomize by placing vertices sequentially where the conditional expected final crossing count is largest. Express this choice using already placed neighbours.
Prove the invariant and efficient computation, then compare with the upper bound of all edges on the optimum. An expected random guarantee alone does not supply the requested deterministic algorithm.
2023B-p3#x: Find a collection of pairwise disjoint hyperedges by repeatedly taking an uncovered hyperedge.
Select all three vertices of each chosen hyperedge. Every vertex cover must pay at least one vertex for each disjoint chosen hyperedge, while your algorithm pays three.
Show the process covers every hyperedge at termination and that chosen witness hyperedges are disjoint. This unweighted argument does not automatically handle arbitrary vertex costs.
2024B-p5#x: Write the weighted hitting-set relaxation with one variable per ground element and one covering constraint per required subset.
Round up every variable at least the reciprocal of the maximum subset size. For a fixed subset, not all its fractional variables can lie below this threshold.
Prove coverage and a weighted cost bound separately. The parameter is the size of a required subset, not the number of subsets containing an element.
2025B-p2#b: Use the weighted set-cover LP from part (a). Here frequency bounds the number of set variables in any one element's constraint.
Select every set whose fractional variable is at least the reciprocal of the frequency. Bound the selected set's cost by frequency times its fractional contribution.
Include equality at the rounding threshold. State the lower-bound relation between LP optimum and integer optimum before concluding the approximation ratio.
2025C-p2#b: Fix an arbitrary element and look at a feasible optimal primal covering solution together with the optimal dual.
The primal coverage constraint implies some containing set has a positive primal variable. Complementary slackness then makes that set's dual inequality tight.
The dual must be optimal, not merely feasible. Show this for every element to conclude that all tight sets form a cover.
2025C-p2#c: Start from the feasible tight-set cover established in part (b), and write its total cost as a sum over selected sets.
Replace each tight set's cost by its sum of dual element prices. Swap summations; each element's price is counted no more than its frequency.
Use nonnegative dual prices and weak duality to compare with the integer optimum. Do not count only one occurrence of an element that belongs to several selected sets.
hw2026s2-p6#a: Choose a nonzero eigenvector and apply the PSD inequality to that particular vector.
The quadratic form becomes the eigenvalue times the vector's positive squared norm. Divide by that norm to infer the eigenvalue's sign.
Use real symmetry and nonzero eigenvectors. Checking diagonal entries alone would not prove the eigenvalue claim.
hw2026s2-p6#b: Diagonalize the symmetric matrix orthogonally. Its nonnegative eigenvalues have real square roots, including zero.
Form a factor from the diagonal square roots and the transposed orthogonal matrix, then multiply its transpose by itself.
Write the factor explicitly and verify multiplication order. The desired factorization is transpose-times-factor, not necessarily the reverse.
hw2026s2-p6#c: Take an arbitrary real vector and insert the proposed factorization into its quadratic form.
The result is a squared Euclidean norm, so it is nonnegative. Also observe that a transpose-times-factor product is symmetric.
Quantify over every real vector. Neither invertibility nor positive definiteness is required.
hw2026s3-p3#a: Fix a nonempty vertex subset and try spreading total vertex mass one uniformly over it.
Set vertex weights to its reciprocal size on that subset and zero elsewhere, with the same weight on its internal edges. Verify the LP rows and calculate its objective.
Match the question's density convention, including any factor of two. A feasible LP point for each subset proves the relaxation upper-bounds the maximum density.
hw2026s3-p3#b: For a fixed feasible vertex-weight vector, inspect the largest allowed value of each edge variable.
Both endpoint constraints cap it by the smaller endpoint weight. Replacing it by that minimum preserves the upper bounds and can only increase an objective with positive edge coefficients.
Check all other constraints before claiming feasibility, and keep the vertex weights unchanged. This is a WLOG statement about a maximization LP.
hw2026s3-p3#c: Use the threshold definitions and the minimum-endpoint identity from part (b) for one fixed edge.
Both endpoints pass a threshold exactly when their minimum weight passes it. This is precisely the edge-threshold condition.
State that the equivalence is for an existing graph edge. Two surviving vertices do not create an edge absent from the original graph.
hw2026s3-p3#f: Subtract the LP objective times the threshold vertex count from the threshold edge count. Use parts (d) and (e) to examine its expectation.

With a normalized optimal vertex-weight total, the difference has mean zero, so a nonempty threshold set must attain nonnegative difference. Justify nonemptiness using positive threshold intervals or the finite list of positive weight breakpoints.
Do not use an empty set to satisfy a vacuous inequality, and do not replace the expectation of a ratio by a ratio of expectations. Explain how to find a suitable breakpoint.
hw2026s4-p3#b: Let one indicator record whether each set is selected by randomized rounding.
Each indicator's expectation is its selection probability, the LP value. Sum these expectations and compare the LP objective with the optimum integer cover cost.
This is an expected size bound, not a proof that the sampled family covers all elements or always has small size.
hw2026s4-p3#c: Fix one element and list all sets that contain it. Its failure event is that none is selected.
Multiply the independent nonselection probabilities, bound each by an exponential, and use the LP constraint that their fractional coverage totals at least one.
Independence is between set selections, not between different elements' coverage events. Take the complement only after bounding noncoverage.
hw2026s4-p3#d: Distinguish the requested error parameter from Euler's number in the printed notation. Begin with one element's failure over repeated independent rounds.
Raise its one-round failure bound to the number of rounds, then union bound over elements. Bound the size of the union by the sum of round sizes and use linearity for its expectation.

Round the number of rounds up and reflect that ceiling in the cost bound. A high-probability cover and expected size bound do not automatically give both guarantees simultaneously at the same constant.
hw2026s4-p4#x: Encode Boolean labels as signs. Write a satisfied equality and a satisfied inequality as expressions involving their sign product.

Replace signs by unit vectors. Under a random hyperplane, use angle-over-pi for unequal labels and its complement for equal labels, then compare each with its relaxed contribution using the given approximation inequality.
Check both equation types, objective weights and the relaxation's bound direction. State that the approximation is in expectation unless you add the required amplification or derandomization.
hw2025s5-p2#x: Select a vertex, add it to the independent set, and delete it together with its remaining neighbours.
Each chosen vertex removes at most one plus the maximum degree vertices. Charge removed vertices to that choice and compare total vertices with any optimum independent set.
Prove independence and account for every vertex exactly once in the deletion process. State the maximization ratio in the direction used by the course.
2017A-p1#e: Hold the accuracy parameter fixed before deciding whether the displayed runtime is polynomial in input size.
For any fixed positive accuracy, the displayed exponent is a constant. Then separately examine what happens when reciprocal accuracy is treated as an input parameter.
Check the approximation guarantee's direction for the optimization problem. Do not require a PTAS to be fully polynomial in reciprocal accuracy.
2014A-p5#x: Introduce an artificial vertex connected at zero cost to every sender. Which terminals must a connecting structure contain?
Use all receivers and the artificial vertex as Steiner terminals, apply the known Steiner approximation, and remove the artificial edges afterward.
Prove optimum costs correspond in both directions and that each remaining receiver component contains a sender. Nonnegative edge costs justify pruning unnecessary cycles or components.
2014A-p8#a: Give every variable an independent fair truth value and one indicator per satisfied clause.

For a clause of three distinct variables, calculate the probability all its literals are false and take the complement. Sum satisfaction expectations and compare with the number of clauses as an optimum upper bound.
Check the clause assumptions and state that the guarantee is in expectation. Overlapping clauses do not prevent linearity.
2014A-p9#a: Take any maximal matching and compare it with an optimum matching. What would an optimum edge disjoint from all selected endpoints imply?
Every optimum edge touches a selected matching edge. Charge it there; each selected edge has two endpoints, and an optimum matching uses each endpoint at most once.
Use maximality only to prove coverage by endpoints. Maximal and maximum are different, and the charging multiplicity gives the factor.
2014B-p7#b: Inspect the last job placed on the machine that ends with maximum load under the least-loaded rule.
Before that placement, its load is at most the average load already placed. Bound the optimum using both the average total load and the largest item, then compare the final makespan.
The objective is minimum capacity with a fixed number of bins, not minimum bin count. Identify which optimum lower bound pays for each term.
2015B-p3#x: Take an optimum tour and consider alternating edges as candidate matchings. Check whether the vertex count is even or odd.
For an even tour, the two alternating perfect matchings split the tour cost. For odd size, use an averaging argument over maximum-cardinality alternating matchings obtained by leaving one vertex out.
Compare with a minimum-weight maximum-cardinality matching, not an arbitrary maximal matching. State the parity case and why a candidate of the required cardinality exists.
2016A-p5#x: Trace the exact greedy rule on a small graph instead of importing a known guarantee for a different max-cut greedy algorithm.
Look for an early local choice that leaves many later edges uncut. Compute both the greedy cut and a concrete better cut; enlarge or adjust the instance if the desired ratio violation is not strict.
Specify vertex order and tie-breaking if the rule permits them. A bad cut alone is insufficient unless the given algorithm actually produces it.
2017B-p2#a: Use a slightly better value-to-weight ratio to force greedy to choose an item that blocks a much more valuable item.

Try capacity one, a tiny item with ratio just above a full-capacity item's ratio, and a full-capacity item of much larger total value. Parameterize the tiny size to make the value ratio arbitrarily bad.
Keep both items individually feasible and make the ordering strict. Check whether the algorithm compares against the best single item; that modified algorithm is a different claim.
2018A-p2#a: Find a required subset not yet hit, and consider selecting all of its at most three elements.
Repeat until every subset is hit. The chosen witness subsets must be disjoint from earlier selected elements, which will supply a lower bound for the analysis.
Describe a polynomial implementation and handle an empty required subset as infeasible. Selecting only one arbitrary element does not give the same proof.
2018A-p2#b: Use the witness subsets selected by the algorithm in part (a), not every subset in the input.
They are pairwise disjoint, so any hitting set needs at least one distinct element for each. Your algorithm pays at most three elements per witness subset.
Prove disjointness from the rule and then derive the cost comparison. Do not assume all input subsets are disjoint.
2018A-p2#c: When a new subset arrives, do nothing if it is already hit; otherwise select all its elements.
The newly unhit witness subsets are disjoint from everything already selected. Compare their number with an offline optimum that must hit all of them.
Selections must be irrevocable and based only on arrivals so far. The lower bound may use the final offline optimum without giving the online algorithm future knowledge.
2018B-p2#a: To refute exact optimality, you only need a graph where a permitted minimum-degree first choice leads to a smaller independent set than another choice.
Try joining local gadgets so one low-degree vertex blocks several vertices that could coexist. Trace every deletion and compare with an explicitly listed larger independent set.
Verify the greedy choice really has minimum current degree at each step. Address ties explicitly; do not claim the optimum merely from an unproved guess.
2018B-p2#b: Each greedy choice deletes itself and all its current neighbours. Bound the size of this deleted group using the original maximum degree.
These groups partition the vertices, so the number chosen is at least total vertices divided by one plus the maximum degree. Compare with the trivial upper bound on an optimum independent set.
Prove the selected vertices are independent and the algorithm runs in polynomial time. Minimum-degree selection is allowed but not needed for this coarse bound.
2021A-p2#4: The student-selection LP uses upper-capacity constraints. Rounding several positive fractional selections upward can overload one course.
Construct an instance and an optimal fractional solution with multiple variables at or above the stated threshold in one capacity row. Compute the rounded row sum explicitly.

Prove the fractional solution is optimal if the statement requires optimal input, and use the exact threshold parameter defined in the question. Feasibility of a fractional point alone may not refute the claim.
2021A-p3#1: Start from the given minimum cycle cover. Turn each cycle into a path by removing one edge.
Order the paths and connect the end of each to the start of the next, including a final connection back to the first. Completeness supplies every connecting edge.
If there is already one cycle, keep it. Explain why every vertex appears exactly once in the final tour and why all computations are polynomial.
2021A-p3#2: Compare the cost of the patched tour with the original cycle cover one removed-and-added edge pair at a time.

Each replacement adds at most one net cost because edges have weights one or two. Bound the number of cycles by one third of the vertex count, and bound optimum below by both the minimum cover cost and the vertex count.
The cycle-count bound assumes cycles have at least three vertices. Check the undirected simple-cycle convention; allowing two-cycles would change this proof.
2021B-p1#4: Focus on a capacity-one vertex incident to several positive fractional edge variables.
Look for an optimal fractional solution with two incident variables at the rounding threshold, so rounding both up exceeds that vertex's capacity. Verify the other-side capacities as well.
Show fractional optimality and use the stated non-strict threshold. An integral optimal solution may exist even though another optimal fractional solution rounds badly.
2021B-p3#1: Process vertices in a fixed order and count already assigned neighbours of each colour.
Assign the new vertex the colour with the fewest already assigned neighbours. This makes at most one third of its backward incident edges monochromatic.
Explain how ties are handled and why the rule is polynomial. Only count edges to previously processed vertices at each step.
2021B-p3#2: Charge each edge when its later endpoint is coloured. At that moment, split backward neighbours into three colour classes.

The least populated class contains at most one third of those neighbours, so at least two thirds of backward edges become properly coloured. Sum over vertices and compare with the optimum's maximum possible edge count.
Count every edge exactly once and preserve the fraction direction for maximization. The algorithm need not produce a proper colouring of the whole graph.
2015A-p6#a: At this stage, group bins by the reciprocal-integer size of their most recently placed items. Use the descending size order.

For any fixed denominator, packing items of that size fills bins in exact increments and can leave at most one unfinished bin of that type under the stated placement rule. Count the possible denominators processed so far.
Use the exact packing rule from the question, not an arbitrary heuristic. Handle already full bins separately from the unfinished ones.
2015A-p6#b: Look at the next item that could not fit in a non-last bin. Its size bounds the unused space left behind.
Use the reciprocal-size ordering and the stage parameter to turn ‘does not fit’ into a lower bound on the load already in that bin.
Track strict versus weak inequalities and why the last bin is exceptional. State which item sizes have already been processed.
2015A-p6#c: Try to show the total weight in all bins is greater than the number of bins minus one.
Combine the unfinished-bin count from part (a) with the load bounds from part (b), accounting for the exceptional final bin. The total item weight is a lower bound on the optimum bin count.
An additive one guarantee is different from a multiplicative approximation ratio. Give the final integer rounding argument and handle a single-bin packing.
2017A-p3#x: Adding a matching on all but two odd-degree tree vertices should leave exactly two odd vertices. Check connectivity and parity first.

Order the tree's odd vertices along an optimal Hamilton path. Construct two candidate matchings, each leaving two of them unmatched, whose total shortcut-edge cost is at most the optimum path cost. The minimum such matching costs at most the cheaper candidate.

Use the triangle inequality, the MST lower bound, and the free-endpoint path setting. Prove the final Euler path can be shortcut without increasing cost; fixed prescribed endpoints would be a different problem.
